figures.alt: Your phone joins the Wi-Fi, the sign-in page stands in the way, and the internet opens after you sign in

figures.caption: **Figure 1. Full bars is only step one.** Your phone joins the Wi-Fi first. The road to the internet stays closed until you finish the page.
figures.alt: Before you sign in, the Wi-Fi works but the road to the internet is closed. After you sign in, it opens

figures.caption: **Figure 2. Four common asks.** Most pages want one of these. Some only want you to tap Accept.
figures.alt: A sign-in page asks for one of four things. None of them is the password to your email

figures.caption: **Figure 3. Why places use one.** Hotels, airports, cafes and planes each have a reason. The page always comes first.
figures.alt: Places put a sign-in page in front of their Wi-Fi to check who you are, show their rules, charge, or share fairly

figures.caption: **Figure 4. A test with a known answer.** A normal network sends the test page back. A sign-in network answers differently, usually by sending you to its own page. Your phone sees the wrong answer and pops the page up for you.
figures.alt: Your phone asks for a test page it already knows. A normal network sends it. A sign-in network sends its sign-in page instead, and your phone pops it up

figures.caption: **Figure 5. Three ways the page shows up.** Each kind of device brings the page to you a little differently. Either way, finish the page.
figures.alt: On an iPhone or iPad a sign-in window opens by itself. On Android a notice asks you to sign in. On a laptop the browser or a notice takes you there

figures.caption: **Figure 6. Start with http://.** A plain http:// address lets the network show its page. A secure https:// site can't be swapped, so your browser warns you instead.
figures.alt: If the page does not pop up, open a browser and type a plain address. A secure site you saved shows a warning instead: do not click past it

figures.caption: **Figure 7. Forget, then join again.** This makes your phone check the network from the start.
figures.alt: If the page still won't show, forget the network and join it again. That gives the check a fresh start

figures.caption: **Figure 8. Off for a moment, then back on.** Switch the VPN off only long enough to finish the page, then turn it back on.
figures.alt: A VPN can hide the sign-in page. Turn it off, sign in, then turn it back on

figures.caption: **Figure 9. Two reasons the page returns.** Your time or pass ran out. Or your phone now shows the network a new Wi-Fi address, so it looks like a new guest.
figures.alt: The page comes back when your time runs out, or when your phone shows the network a new Wi-Fi address and looks like a new guest

figures.caption: **Figure 10. Outside and inside.** Most sites now use secure pages, marked with a padlock. The network usually sees which site you visit, unless a VPN or a privacy setting hides it. It doesn't see what's on the page.
figures.alt: The network can see which sites you visit and how much you use. On secure pages it can't see what you read or type

figures.caption: **Figure 11. A real page, and a trap.** A real page asks for a room number, a code, a login the place gave you, or a pass. A trap asks for the password to your email.
figures.alt: A real sign-in page asks for a room number, a code, or to pay for a pass. A page that asks for your email password is a trap

figures.caption: **Figure 12. Check the network name.** A look-alike name can be a trap. Join the one the staff or the sign names.
figures.alt: Two networks can have almost the same name. Ask the staff or read the sign, and join the one they name

figures.caption: **Figure 13. No screen, no sign-in.** Ask whether the front desk can add your device. Or bring a travel router: it signs in once, and your devices join it.
figures.alt: A TV stick, a game console or a smart speaker may have no way to show the sign-in page. Ask the front desk, or use a travel router

figures.caption: **Figure 14. What the bars measure.** Full bars say you hear the Wi-Fi well. They say nothing about the internet.
figures.alt: The Wi-Fi bars only tell you how well you hear the access point. They say nothing about the internet

figures.caption: **Figure 15. Arriving and leaving.** Finish the page before you count on your apps. Forget the network when you go.
figures.alt: Finish the page before you count on email, messages or Wi-Fi Calling. When you leave, forget the network
